title: Objective comparison on one problem (e.g. classical vs power-mean): does the objective change the answer?
summary: The objective you minimise changes the answer. The same data are fitted with two objectives (a classical sum of squares and a robust alternative) under the same budget, and the fits and their errors are shown together.

media.alt: Left: a scatter of noisy decaying data with three outliers, a dashed blue curve (objective A, classical) lying above the data trend and a solid teal curve (objective B, robust) following it. Right: two bars, A at 0.276 and B at 0.007, titled same data same budget.
media.caption: Reference render of class F7.5 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: Does the objective change the answer?
read_the_figure.axes: Left: time in seconds (0 to 10) against signal in arbitrary units. Right: a categorical axis A and B against the RMSE to the true curve (0 to about 0.33).
look_at: Are both fits made on exactly the same data and the same number of evaluations?
Which points does each fit follow, and which points pull the classical fit away?
What is the error measure on the right and what is it measured against?
Can the true curve be known in a real problem, or only in a synthetic test?
as_drawn: Sixty points of a decaying exponential plus noise, with three outliers added (+1.3 at t of about 1.4, -1.1 at about 4.3, and +1.5 at about 6.9). A budget of 300 evaluations each is noted on the plot.
Objective A (classical, dashed blue) is pulled above the trend over most of the range. Objective B (robust, solid teal) lies on the trend.
The bar chart gives the RMSE to the true curve: A 0.276 and B 0.007, a factor of about 40.
The robust fit in this demonstration is the true curve plus a 0.01 wiggle, so the 0.007 is built in: the figure shows the form, not the outcome of a real optimizer.
read_the_figure.proves: On this data, with these outliers and this budget, the objective changed the fitted curve and its error against the truth. Whether the same holds for other data or noise needs more examples; the truth is only available in a synthetic test.
if_wrong: Different data or different budgets for the two fits: the comparison measures something else.
Error measured against the data and not against the truth: a robust fit is then penalised for ignoring the outliers.
A truth curve unavailable (a real problem): replace the RMSE to truth by a held-out error.
must_check: same data: otherwise the difference may come from the data, not the objective.
equal budget: otherwise the difference may come from computing effort, not the objective.

terms.meaning: The quantity an optimizer minimises to fit a model to data.
The classical objective: the mean of squared residuals.
An objective that limits the influence of outliers, such as the absolute value or a power mean with exponent below 2.
The p-th root of the mean of |r|^p; p = 2 is the RMS, p = 1 the mean absolute value, and p large approaches the maximum.
A data point far from the trend, for example from a faulty measurement.
Root mean square difference between a fitted curve and the exact curve; possible only when the truth is known.

remember: Least squares gives every residual a weight proportional to its size, so outliers pull hard.
Mean breaks with one outlier; the median does not.
Power mean: M_p grows with p; large p is dominated by the worst residual.
Compare objectives on the same data and budget.
Measure error against the truth or a held-out set, not against the training data.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Left panel: grey dots are the data, a dashed blue line the fit of the classical objective, a solid teal line the fit of the robust objective; line style and colour both differ. Right panel: bar heights are the errors with numbers printed above each bar. The panel title restates the two conditions that make the comparison fair.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: Plain language: what you ask an optimizer to minimise defines what 'best' means. A few wild points can drag a fit that is judged by squared errors because a point five times further away counts twenty-five times as much. Putting the two fits on the same data, with the same effort, makes the effect of the objective, and nothing else, visible, and the bars turn the visual difference into a number.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: A truth curve exists only in a synthetic example, so the bar chart cannot be reproduced on real data. A single data set with three hand-placed outliers is an extreme case that favours the robust objective; with clean Gaussian noise the classical fit is more efficient. The factor of 40 depends on the number and size of the outliers. And the 'equal budget' says nothing about whether each optimizer converged.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: Plot the residuals of both fits so the outliers are visible. Use a held-out set or cross-validation for the error. A sweep over the power-mean exponent p, from 2 down to 0.5, shows how the fit moves continuously from classical to very robust. A table of the median and the largest error over many random data sets is better evidence than one example.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Add the residuals of both fits as a strip below, repeat with 100 random data sets and show the distribution of the error for each objective as two box plots, and mark the outliers in a different colour.

steps.title: The power mean
steps.note: Non-decreasing in p. For residuals 0.1, 0.1, 0.1, 0.1, 3 it gives 0.36 (p = 0.5), 0.68 (p = 1), 1.34 (p = 2), 2.0 (p = 4), 2.9 (p = 50) and 3.0 (maximum).

steps.title: Outlier influence on mean and median
steps.note: One outlier moves the mean by 0.8 and the median not at all: the breakdown point of the mean is 0, of the median 50 percent.

steps.title: Error against the truth
steps.note: Possible only if y_true is known, as in the synthetic render; on real data use a held-out error.

worked.title: Reading the objective comparison in the reference render
worked.problem: (1) What are the two RMSE values and their ratio? (2) Which points pull fit A away from the trend and in which direction? (3) What does the power mean tell you about the weight an outlier has?

solution.text: (2) Two of the three outliers are high (+1.3 near t = 1.4 and +1.5 near t = 6.9) and one is low (-1.1 near t = 4.3); the net effect is a pull upward, which lifts fit A above the trend over most of the range.
(3) With residuals 0.1, 0.1, 0.1, 0.1 and 3, the power mean rises from 0.36 at p = 0.5 to 1.34 at p = 2 as the outlier's weight grows.

worked.answer: RMSE 0.276 against 0.007, a ratio of about 40 (in a demonstration whose robust fit is built from the truth); the outliers lift fit A; the lower the power-mean exponent, the less the one outlier counts.

analyze.q: Why would the classical objective be better with clean Gaussian noise?
The robust fit lies almost exactly on the truth. Why should you be suspicious of that in a real study?
analyze.hint: Synthetic construction; the same would not happen with real noise.

analyze.q: What extra panel would convince a sceptical reader?

evaluate.q: A study reports that a robust objective cuts the error 40-fold. What do you ask?
evaluate.hint: Number and size of outliers, data realism, baselines.

create: Fit the same data with power-mean exponents 2, 1 and 0.5 and plot all three curves.
Repeat with 100 random outlier patterns and plot the distribution of the RMSE for the two objectives.

checks.q: Why does an outlier pull a least-squares fit harder than a mean-absolute fit?
checks.answer: The squared residual grows as the square of the distance, so one far point can outweigh many near ones; the absolute value grows only linearly.

checks.q: Residuals 0.2, 0.2, 0.2, 2.0. Compute the p = 1 and p = 2 power means.
The bars compare errors to the true curve. Why can that not be done in a real application and what would you use?
checks.answer: The true curve is unknown, so use a held-out or cross-validated error, and judge robustness with residual plots and repeated data sets.
